catalog_quote: No relevant tones were observed. There is great confusion of stress (e. g. 1 m'usa: 3 muṣ'a, 1 'ānda: 3 ānd'a), and it is not possible to lay down any rules regarding its place. Note, however, 1,3 b'uṛa grandfather; buṛ'a deaf.

audit.recode_to: Fixed final (default word-final stress; the only pattern in uninflected nouns), with morphologically conditioned non-final stress: case/inflectional suffixes do not take stress, so inflected forms keep stress on the root (/ˈgələ/ 'valley-LOC' vs /gəˈlə/ 'hill'), making stress 'only partly contrastive' on the surface. Deciding source: Liljegren & Soan 2025, JIPA 55:146-147. Keep Morgenstierne 1950:9 as a historical note (inter-informant variation; b'uṛa vs buṛ'a pair).

sources.quote: 'Stress is only partly contrastive in Gawarbati. The most frequent stress pattern is one with main stress on the final syllable. This is also the only stress pattern found as far as uninflected nouns are concerned. It is, however, possible to find minimal pairs exemplifying stress contrasts if we compare words across inflectional paradigms' (e.g. /ˈgələ/ 'into the valley', case-inflected form of /gəl/ 'valley', where 'stress remains on the root', vs /gəˈlə/ 'hill', 'a non-inflected disyllabic noun, with its "default" stress on its final ... syllable'; likewise /ˈdəntə/ 'in the tooth' vs /dənˈt

sources.note: Modern JIPA Illustration with an explicit stress section and acoustic measurements; states default final stress (sole pattern in uninflected nouns) with root stress retained under case inflection, whereas our coding ('variable, no rule') rests on Morgenstierne's 1950 two-sentence remark about inter-informant confusion.
